documentation.title: Loaded sliding across a FACETED curved surface, with averaged nodal normals
documentation.description:
The testcase for normalSmoothing="nodal". It is ContactSlidingCurved2d with exactly one thing changed: the primary surface no longer reproduces its curve, it approximates it by straight facets. A LINE3 reproduces a parabola exactly if its mid node sits on the parabola; here the mid node sits on the CHORD, so the surface is a polyline whose normal is piecewise constant with a jump at every element boundary. Same element types, material, drive and equilibrium invariant, so a difference between the two testcases can only be the faceting.
The block's facet boundaries COINCIDE with primary facet boundaries initially, and the drive slides it 2.5 facets, ending exactly half a facet out of phase -- the worst case -- so every one of its elements then has a primary facet boundary strictly inside it.
WHAT IT ASSERTS
1. contactForceY = 1.8e7 = 3e7 * 0.6, the vertical equilibrium of the secondary body, whatever the faceting does to the pressure distribution. 2. numCells 6 -> 12, numPoints 12 -> 24, numContactElements 6 -> 12, doubled by the half-facet phase shift. Frozen under slidingType="small". 3. contactForceX. NOT an equilibrium statement -- it is whatever the u_x reaction balances -- but it is what pins normalSmoothing="nodal", coming out measurably different with "none".
WHAT MEASURING IT FOUND. A faceted normal was expected to STALL Newton, g_N not being differentiable where a point crosses a facet boundary. It does not: a jumping normal costs iterations and monotonicity, not convergence, because the discontinuity is in the DIRECTION of a converged traction and the point positions themselves converge. What smoothing does buy is that the answer stops depending on where the integration points happen to sit -- with smoothing the two segmentations agree to 4-5 digits, with facet normals they disagree, and the coarser the facets the more. Iterations improve too, but not uniformly, which is why this testcase asserts the resultant and the counts rather than an iteration count.
The load is higher than ContactSlidingCurved2d's because two polylines half a facet out of phase differ by a saw-tooth, and the elastic deflection must reach that amplitude for the patch to cover the interface rather than perch on the high points.
